items.stem: Which type of wave can be polarised?
items.answer: Transverse
items.markingKey: Transverse (A1). Oscillation direction must be perpendicular to travel.

items.stem: Briefly explain why sound cannot travel through space.
items.answer: Sound is a mechanical, longitudinal wave that propagates by collisions between particles of a medium; in a vacuum there are no particles.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sound is a mechanical, longitudinal wave that propagates by collisions between particles of a medium; in a vacuum there are no particles. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of the following statements about transverse and longitudinal travelling waves is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Lars.)
options: Waves transfer matter from one place to another.
Mechanical waves do, but electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum.
Speed depends on the medium, not the amplitude (for small amplitudes).
All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum; gamma photons have higher energy because of their higher frequency.
items.answer: Waves transfer matter from one place to another.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: Waves transfer energy; particles of the medium oscillate about their equilibrium positions.

items.stem: A student claims: "Waves transfer matter from one place to another." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Waves transfer energy; particles of the medium oscillate about their equilibrium positions.
items.markingKey: Waves transfer energy; particles of the medium oscillate about their equilibrium positions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A tsunami travels 500 km across the ocean at 200 m s⁻¹. Calculate the travel time in hours.

This question is about transverse and longitudinal travelling waves.

(a) A seismometer in Nairobi records P-waves (7.0 km s⁻¹) and then S-waves (4.5 km s⁻¹) 60 s later from the same earthquake. Calculate the distance to the epicentre. [3]

(b) Explain how seismic waves provide evidence that Earth’s outer core is liquid. [3]

(c) Outline one argument for and one against the statement: "Early-warning systems based on detecting P-waves can significantly reduce earthquake casualties." [4]
items.answer: (a) 756 km (b) Transverse S-waves are not detected in a shadow zone on the far side of Earth; since liquids cannot transmit shear (transverse) waves, the outer core must be liquid. (c) They provide valuable seconds that can save lives and infrastructure, particularly for automated responses, but are limited close to the epicentre.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] d/4.5 − d/7.0 = 60 (M1); d = 756 km (A1). (b) [3 marks] Transverse S-waves are not detected in a shadow zone on the far side of Earth; since liquids cannot transmit shear (transverse) waves, the outer core must be liquid. (c) [4 marks] For: P-waves travel faster than the damaging S- and surface waves, giving seconds of warning; automatic train stopping and gas shut-off in Japan and Mexico. Against: warning time is short close to the epicentre; false alarms reduce public trust; expensive dense sensor networks are needed. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: They provide valuable seconds that can save lives and infrastructure, particularly for automated responses, but are limited close to the epicentre.

items.stem: As a wave passes, the particles of the medium
options: move in straight lines away from the source
items.answer: oscillate about fixed positions
items.markingKey: B. No net transfer of matter.

items.stem: A transverse wave travels to the right along a rope. A point on the rope moves
items.answer: up and down
items.markingKey: C. Perpendicular to travel.

items.stem: Explain the difference between longitudinal waves and transverse waves.
items.answer: In transverse waves the medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (crests and troughs, can be polarised); in longitudinal waves it oscillates parallel to it (compressions and rarefactions, cannot be polarised).
items.markingKey: In transverse waves the medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (crests and troughs, can be polarised); in longitudinal waves it oscillates parallel to it (compressions and rarefactions, cannot be polarised). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "In a longitudinal wave the particles move along with the wave." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: They oscillate back and forth about fixed positions parallel to the direction of travel.
items.markingKey: They oscillate back and forth about fixed positions parallel to the direction of travel. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: An earthquake occurs 150 km from Melbourne. P-waves travel at 6.0 km s⁻¹ and S-waves at 4.5 km s⁻¹. Calculate the time between the arrivals of the two waves.
An earthquake occurs 150 km from Oslo. P-waves travel at 7.0 km s⁻¹ and S-waves at 3.8 km s⁻¹. Calculate the time between the arrivals of the two waves.
A seismometer in Kuala Lumpur records P-waves (7.0 km s⁻¹) and then S-waves (3.5 km s⁻¹) 60 s later from the same earthquake. Calculate the distance to the epicentre.
items.answer: 420 km

items.stem: "Early-warning systems based on detecting P-waves can significantly reduce earthquake casualties." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: They provide valuable seconds that can save lives and infrastructure, particularly for automated responses, but are limited close to the epicentre.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: P-waves travel faster than the damaging S- and surface waves, giving seconds of warning; automatic train stopping and gas shut-off in Japan and Mexico. Arguments against: warning time is short close to the epicentre; false alarms reduce public trust; expensive dense sensor networks are needed. Supported judgement: They provide valuable seconds that can save lives and infrastructure, particularly for automated responses, but are limited close to the epicentre. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: An earthquake produces P-waves (6.0 km s⁻¹) and S-waves (3.5 km s⁻¹). A seismometer in a city records the S-waves arriving 48 s after the P-waves. (a) State which wave is longitudinal. (b) Determine the distance to the epicentre. (c) Calculate the warning time a P-wave alert could give before the S-waves arrive at a city 200 km from the epicentre. (d) Explain why at least three stations are needed to locate the epicentre.
items.answer: (a) P-waves; (b) d/3.5 − d/6.0 = 48, d = 403 km; (c) 200/3.5 − 200/6.0 = 23.8 s (less processing time); (d) each station gives a distance (a circle); three circles intersect at one point.
items.markingKey: (a) P-waves; (b) d/3.5 − d/6.0 = 48, d = 403 km; (c) 200/3.5 − 200/6.0 = 23.8 s (less processing time); (d) each station gives a distance (a circle); three circles intersect at one point.

items.stem: A wave of frequency 50 Hz has a wavelength of 4.0 m. Its speed is
items.answer: 200 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: D. v = fλ.

items.stem: Briefly explain why increasing the frequency of a signal generator connected to a vibrating string reduces the wavelength.
items.answer: The wave speed depends on the string’s tension and mass per unit length, which are unchanged; with v constant, λ = v/f decreases as f increases.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The wave speed depends on the string’s tension and mass per unit length, which are unchanged; with v constant, λ = v/f decreases as f increases. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student in Geneva is checking notes on wave speed, frequency and wavelength: v = fλ. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Radio waves are electromagnetic; a radio receiver converts the information they carry into sound.
All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum; gamma photons have higher energy because of their higher frequency.
Increasing the frequency of a wave increases its speed.
Speed depends on the medium, not the amplitude (for small amplitudes).
items.answer: Increasing the frequency of a wave increases its speed.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: In a given medium the speed is fixed; increasing frequency reduces the wavelength.

items.stem: Ripples in a tank have a wavelength of 3.5 cm and a frequency of 8 Hz. Calculate their speed.
Water waves of frequency 10 Hz travel at 0.3 m s⁻¹ in deep water and slow to 0.18 m s⁻¹ in shallow water. Calculate the wavelength in the shallow water.
items.markingKey: f unchanged (M1); λ = v/f = 0.0180 m (A1).

items.stem:
A loudspeaker connected to a signal generator emits sound of frequency f. The wavelength λ is found by moving a microphone between adjacent points where the signal is in phase, using a dual-trace oscilloscope. Theory: λ = v/f.

f / Hz | λ / m
400 | 0.871
500 | 0.696
600 | 0.574
800 | 0.432
1000 | 0.346
1200 | 0.284

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the speed of sound v in air. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±2 %. State v with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) λ (y) against 1/f (x); (b) gradient ≈ 351 m s⁻¹; (c) 351 m s⁻¹; (d) (351 ± 7) m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) λ (y) against 1/f (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 351 m s⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) v = gradient = 351 m s⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 2 % of the value = 7 m s⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "5G mobile networks use higher frequencies so they must transmit data faster through the air."
items.answer: The waves are no faster; higher frequencies give greater bandwidth (data rate) but shorter range.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher carrier frequencies allow greater bandwidth, so more data per second. Arguments against: all EM waves travel at the same speed in air; higher frequencies have shorter range and are absorbed more by buildings; requires more base stations. Supported judgement: The waves are no faster; higher frequencies give greater bandwidth (data rate) but shorter range.

items.stem: A student uses a ripple tank with a vibrating dipper at 12 Hz. A photograph shows 9 complete wavefronts spanning 24.0 cm in the deep region and 9 spanning 15.6 cm in the shallow region. (a) Calculate the wavelength in each region. (b) Calculate the wave speed in each region. (c) State and explain what happens to the frequency at the boundary. (d) Suggest one source of uncertainty and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) 9 wavefronts span 8 wavelengths: 3.00 cm and 1.95 cm; (b) 0.360 m s⁻¹ and 0.234 m s⁻¹; (c) unchanged – set by the dipper; (d) wavefronts blurred in the photo – use a stroboscope to freeze the pattern and measure across more waves.
items.markingKey: (a) 9 wavefronts span 8 wavelengths: 3.00 cm and 1.95 cm; (b) 0.360 m s⁻¹ and 0.234 m s⁻¹; (c) unchanged – set by the dipper; (d) wavefronts blurred in the photo – use a stroboscope to freeze the pattern and measure across more waves.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The number of complete oscillations per second of any point on the wave, f, in Hz"?
items.answer: frequency (wave)
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of frequency (wave).

items.stem: Define the term "wavelength".
items.answer: The shortest distance between two points on a wave that are in phase, λ, in m
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the shortest distance between two points on a wave that are in phase, λ, in m. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between the wave speed and the speed of particles in the medium.
items.answer: The wave speed is the rate at which energy propagates (v = fλ, fixed by the medium); the particle speed varies during each oscillation, depends on amplitude and frequency, and is maximum at equilibrium.
items.markingKey: The wave speed is the rate at which energy propagates (v = fλ, fixed by the medium); the particle speed varies during each oscillation, depends on amplitude and frequency, and is maximum at equilibrium. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
This question is about wave speed, frequency and wavelength: v = fλ.

(a) Calculate the frequency of light of wavelength 450 nm in a vacuum. [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain why the frequency of a wave does not change when it moves into a different medium. [3]

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "displacement–distance graph"?
options: The speed at which energy is transferred by the wave, v = fλ
A point of maximum negative displacement on a transverse wave
A wave in which the oscillations of the medium are parallel to the direction of energy transfer
A "snapshot" graph showing the displacement of every point along a wave at one instant; the wavelength can be read from it
items.answer: A "snapshot" graph showing the displacement of every point along a wave at one instant; the wavelength can be read from it
items.markingKey: D. "displacement–distance graph" is a "snapshot" graph showing the displacement of every point along a wave at one instant; the wavelength can be read from it.

items.stem: On a displacement–time graph for a point on a wave, the gradient gives the
items.answer: velocity of that point
items.markingKey: D. dy/dt.

items.stem: "Two points a full wavelength apart are in antiphase." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: They are in phase (phase difference 2π); points half a wavelength apart are in antiphase.
items.markingKey: They are in phase (phase difference 2π); points half a wavelength apart are in antiphase. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Two points on a wave of frequency 10 Hz reach maximum displacement 0.01 s apart. Calculate their phase difference in degrees.
A displacement–distance graph shows 4 complete wavelengths in 3.0 m. A displacement–time graph for one point shows a period of 0.25 s. Calculate the wave speed.
Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Graphs are a better way than equations to describe waves."
items.answer: Graphs and equations complement each other: graphs aid understanding and data reading, equations allow precise calculation.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: graphs make wavelength, period and phase visible; easy to compare snapshots. Arguments against: equations y = A sin(2π(x/λ − t/T)) contain all information compactly; calculations need equations; graphs can be misread (confusing the two types). Supported judgement: Graphs and equations complement each other: graphs aid understanding and data reading, equations allow precise calculation.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A point of maximum positive displacement on a transverse wave"?
items.answer: crest
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of crest.

items.stem: Distinguish between a displacement–time graph and a displacement–distance graph.
items.answer: A displacement–distance graph is a snapshot of all points at one instant and shows the wavelength; a displacement–time graph follows one point over time and shows the period.
items.markingKey: A displacement–distance graph is a snapshot of all points at one instant and shows the wavelength; a displacement–time graph follows one point over time and shows the period. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how compressions can be identified on a displacement–distance graph of a longitudinal wave.
items.answer: A compression is where particles on either side are displaced towards the point: positive displacement to the left of the point and negative to the right, which occurs where the graph crosses zero with negative gradient (taking positive as the direction of travel).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A compression is where particles on either side are displaced towards the point: positive displacement to the left of the point and negative to the right, which occurs where the graph crosses zero with negative gradient (taking positive as the direction of travel). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A teacher in Singapore asks a class to choose the one correct statement about displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs of waves. Which statement should be chosen?
options: At a crest the displacement is maximum and the point is momentarily at rest; points at equilibrium move fastest.
A larger amplitude wave travels faster.
The wavelength is the distance between a crest and the next trough.
items.answer: At a crest the displacement is maximum and the point is momentarily at rest; points at equilibrium move fastest.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. At a crest the displacement is maximum and the point is momentarily at rest; points at equilibrium move fastest.

items.stem: Two points on a wave of wavelength 0.8 m are 0.300 m apart along the direction of travel. Calculate their phase difference in radians.
items.answer: 2.36 rad
items.markingKey: D. Δφ = 2πΔx/λ (M1) = 2.36 rad (A1).

items.stem: "A displacement–time graph shows the shape of the wave." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It shows how one point moves in time; the shape of the wave in space at an instant is shown by a displacement–distance graph.
items.markingKey: It shows how one point moves in time; the shape of the wave in space at an instant is shown by a displacement–distance graph. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: At t = 0 the displacement of a wave is y = 0.05 sin(2πx/0.4) (y and x in m). Calculate the displacement at x = 0.0500 m.

This question is about displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs of waves.

(a) Two points on a wave of wavelength 2.0 m are 0.750 m apart along the direction of travel. Calculate their phase difference in radians. [2]

(b) Explain how the direction of motion of a point on a transverse wave can be found from a displacement–distance graph. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Graphs are a better way than equations to describe waves." [4]
items.answer: (a) 2.36 rad (b) Shift the snapshot a small distance in the direction of travel; the point moves to the displacement of the wave that now occupies its position, so points ahead of a crest move up and points behind it move down. (c) Graphs and equations complement each other: graphs aid understanding and data reading, equations allow precise calculation.

(b) [3 marks] Shift the snapshot a small distance in the direction of travel; the point moves to the displacement of the wave that now occupies its position, so points ahead of a crest move up and points behind it move down. (c) [4 marks] For: graphs make wavelength, period and phase visible; easy to compare snapshots. Against: equations y = A sin(2π(x/λ − t/T)) contain all information compactly; calculations need equations; graphs can be misread (confusing the two types). Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Graphs and equations complement each other: graphs aid understanding and data reading, equations allow precise calculation.

items.stem: A transverse wave of amplitude 3.0 cm, wavelength 0.80 m and frequency 5.0 Hz travels in the +x direction along a rope. At t = 0 the point at x = 0 is at zero displacement moving upwards. (a) Calculate the wave speed. (b) Sketch the displacement–distance graph at t = 0 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 1.6 m. (c) Sketch the displacement–time graph for the point at x = 0 for one period. (d) Determine the phase difference between points at x = 0 and x = 0.20 m and the displacement of the point at x = 0.20 m at t = 0.
items.answer: (a) 4.0 m s⁻¹; (b) two full wavelengths; at x = 0, y = 0 with the wave ahead (x > 0) at y = −3.0 sin(2πx/0.80); (c) sine curve, period 0.20 s, starting at 0 going up; (d) π/2 rad (a quarter wavelength); the point at x = 0.20 m lags by a quarter cycle, so it is at −3.0 cm (a trough) at t = 0.
items.markingKey: (a) 4.0 m s⁻¹; (b) two full wavelengths; at x = 0, y = 0 with the wave ahead (x > 0) at y = −3.0 sin(2πx/0.80); (c) sine curve, period 0.20 s, starting at 0 going up; (d) π/2 rad (a quarter wavelength); the point at x = 0.20 m lags by a quarter cycle, so it is at −3.0 cm (a trough) at t = 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "range of human hearing"?
options: A graph showing how the displacement of one point on a wave varies with time; the period can be read from it
Approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz, decreasing at the upper end with age
The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its equilibrium position
A wave in which the oscillations of the medium are parallel to the direction of energy transfer
items.answer: Approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz, decreasing at the upper end with age
items.markingKey: B. "range of human hearing" is approximately 20 Hz to 20 kHz, decreasing at the upper end with age.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the speed of sound in air increases with temperature.
items.answer: Sound is transmitted by molecular collisions; at higher temperature molecules move faster (c_rms ∝ √T), so disturbances are passed on more quickly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Sound is transmitted by molecular collisions; at higher temperature molecules move faster (c_rms ∝ √T), so disturbances are passed on more quickly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A medical ultrasound scanner operates at 5.0 MHz. The speed of sound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹. Calculate the wavelength in tissue.
During a storm near Vienna, thunder is heard 4.5 s after the lightning flash. Estimate the distance to the lightning (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹).
items.markingKey: A. d = vt (light travel time negligible) (M1) = 1530 m (A1).

items.stem: A ship’s sonar sends a 40 kHz ultrasound pulse vertically down. The echo from the sea bed returns after 0.280 s. The speed of sound in sea water is 1530 m s⁻¹. (a) Calculate the depth of the sea. (b) Calculate the wavelength of the ultrasound in water. (c) Explain why ultrasound rather than audible sound is used. (d) Suggest why the speed of sound in the sea varies with depth.
items.answer: (a) 1530 × 0.280/2 = 214 m; (b) 3.83 cm; (c) shorter wavelength gives better resolution and a narrower beam, and it does not disturb people; (d) temperature, salinity and pressure change with depth.
items.markingKey: (a) 1530 × 0.280/2 = 214 m; (b) 3.83 cm; (c) shorter wavelength gives better resolution and a narrower beam, and it does not disturb people; (d) temperature, salinity and pressure change with depth.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The range of electromagnetic waves ordered by wavelength: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma"?
items.answer: electromagnetic spectrum
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of electromagnetic spectrum.

items.stem: Mohammed writes four statements while revising sound waves and electromagnetic waves: nature and speed. Which one is a misconception?
options: Speed depends on the medium, not the amplitude (for small amplitudes).
Mechanical waves do, but electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum.
Sound travels faster in water (~1500 m s⁻¹) because water is much less compressible; stiffness matters more than density.
Radio waves are a type of sound wave.
items.answer: Radio waves are a type of sound wave.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: Radio waves are electromagnetic; a radio receiver converts the information they carry into sound.

items.stem: A student claims: "Sound travels faster in air than in water because air is less dense." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Sound travels faster in water (~1500 m s⁻¹) because water is much less compressible; stiffness matters more than density.
items.markingKey: Sound travels faster in water (~1500 m s⁻¹) because water is much less compressible; stiffness matters more than density. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves because they have more energy." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum; gamma photons have higher energy because of their higher frequency.
items.markingKey: All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum; gamma photons have higher energy because of their higher frequency. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Electromagnetic radiation has a frequency of 1.00 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Calculate its wavelength in a vacuum.
items.markingKey: D. λ = c/f (M1) = 3.00 × 10⁻⁷ m – ultraviolet region (A1).

items.stem: "Ultrasound imaging is safer than X-ray imaging and should always be preferred." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Ultrasound is preferred where it gives adequate images (pregnancy, soft tissue), but X-rays remain necessary for bone and some diagnoses.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ultrasound is non-ionising – no known cancer risk; real-time imaging, cheap and portable. Arguments against: ultrasound cannot image through bone or air well (lungs, brain); lower resolution for some applications; X-ray CT gives detailed 3D images of bone. Supported judgement: Ultrasound is preferred where it gives adequate images (pregnancy, soft tissue), but X-rays remain necessary for bone and some diagnoses. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "amplitude (wave)"?
options: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its equilibrium position
A wave in which the oscillations of the medium are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer
A disturbance that transfers energy (and information) from one place to another without a net transfer of matter
Sound waves with frequencies above the upper limit of human hearing (about 20 kHz)
items.answer: The maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its equilibrium position
items.markingKey: A. "amplitude (wave)" is the maximum displacement of a point on the wave from its equilibrium position.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A wave that requires a material medium to travel through"?
items.answer: mechanical wave
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of mechanical wave.

items.stem: On a displacement–distance graph of a wave, the distance between two adjacent crests is the
items.answer: wavelength
items.markingKey: D. Snapshot shows λ.

items.stem: Distinguish between electromagnetic waves and sound waves.
items.answer: Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves that need a medium and travel at hundreds to thousands of m s⁻¹; EM waves are transverse oscillating fields that travel through a vacuum at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹.
items.markingKey: Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves that need a medium and travel at hundreds to thousands of m s⁻¹; EM waves are transverse oscillating fields that travel through a vacuum at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Yusuf and a classmate in Dubai disagree about wave speed, frequency and wavelength: v = fλ. Which statement is correct?
options: In a given medium the speed is fixed; increasing frequency reduces the wavelength.
Points at a crest are moving fastest.
Increasing the frequency of a wave increases its speed.
Sound travels faster in air than in water because air is less dense.
items.answer: In a given medium the speed is fixed; increasing frequency reduces the wavelength.
items.markingKey: A. The other options are common misconceptions. In a given medium the speed is fixed; increasing frequency reduces the wavelength.

items.stem: Distinguish between transverse waves and longitudinal waves.
items.answer: In transverse waves the medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (crests and troughs, can be polarised); in longitudinal waves it oscillates parallel to it (compressions and rarefactions, cannot be polarised).
items.markingKey: In transverse waves the medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (crests and troughs, can be polarised); in longitudinal waves it oscillates parallel to it (compressions and rarefactions, cannot be polarised). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student in Vienna is checking notes on displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs of waves. Which statement is incorrect?
options: Speed depends on the medium, not the amplitude (for small amplitudes).
Two points a full wavelength apart are in antiphase.
At a crest the displacement is maximum and the point is momentarily at rest; points at equilibrium move fastest.
Sound travels faster in water (~1500 m s⁻¹) because water is much less compressible; stiffness matters more than density.
items.answer: Two points a full wavelength apart are in antiphase.
items.markingKey: B. This is incorrect: They are in phase (phase difference 2π); points half a wavelength apart are in antiphase.

items.stem: A sound wave passes from air into water. Its wavelength
items.answer: increases
items.markingKey: C. Speed increases, f unchanged.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the speed of particles in the medium and the wave speed.
items.answer: The wave speed is the rate at which energy propagates (v = fλ, fixed by the medium); the particle speed varies during each oscillation, depends on amplitude and frequency, and is maximum at equilibrium.
items.markingKey: The wave speed is the rate at which energy propagates (v = fλ, fixed by the medium); the particle speed varies during each oscillation, depends on amplitude and frequency, and is maximum at equilibrium. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An earthquake occurs 150 km from Melbourne. P-waves travel at 6.5 km s⁻¹ and S-waves at 3.5 km s⁻¹. Calculate the time between the arrivals of the two waves.
A student claims: "A displacement–time graph shows the shape of the wave." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It shows how one point moves in time; the shape of the wave in space at an instant is shown by a displacement–distance graph.
items.markingKey: It shows how one point moves in time; the shape of the wave in space at an instant is shown by a displacement–distance graph. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A medical ultrasound scanner operates at 2.0 MHz. The speed of sound in soft tissue is 1540 m s⁻¹. Calculate the wavelength in tissue.

A loudspeaker connected to a signal generator emits sound of frequency f. The wavelength λ is found by moving a microphone between adjacent points where the signal is in phase, using a dual-trace oscilloscope. Theory: λ = v/f.

f / Hz | λ / m
400 | 0.854
500 | 0.681
600 | 0.567
800 | 0.417
1000 | 0.343
1200 | 0.287

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the speed of sound v in air. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±4 %. State v with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) λ (y) against 1/f (x); (b) gradient ≈ 341 m s⁻¹; (c) 341 m s⁻¹; (d) (340 ± 10) m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) λ (y) against 1/f (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 341 m s⁻¹ – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) v = gradient = 341 m s⁻¹ (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 4 % of the value = 10 m s⁻¹; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: A seismometer in Dubai records P-waves (6.5 km s⁻¹) and then S-waves (4.0 km s⁻¹) 60 s later from the same earthquake. Calculate the distance to the epicentre.
items.answer: 624 km

Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "5G mobile networks use higher frequencies so they must transmit data faster through the air."
items.answer: The waves are no faster; higher frequencies give greater bandwidth (data rate) but shorter range.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher carrier frequencies allow greater bandwidth, so more data per second. Arguments against: all EM waves travel at the same speed in air; higher frequencies have shorter range and are absorbed more by buildings; requires more base stations. Supported judgement: The waves are no faster; higher frequencies give greater bandwidth (data rate) but shorter range.

items.stem:
This question is about transverse and longitudinal travelling waves.

(a) A seismometer in Lisbon records P-waves (6.0 km s⁻¹) and then S-waves (3.8 km s⁻¹) 45 s later from the same earthquake. Calculate the distance to the epicentre. [3]

(b) Explain the difference between transverse waves and longitudinal waves. [4]

(c) "Early-warning systems based on detecting P-waves can significantly reduce earthquake casualties." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of transverse and longitudinal travelling waves. [4]
items.answer: (a) 466 km (b) In transverse waves the medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (crests and troughs, can be polarised); in longitudinal waves it oscillates parallel to it (compressions and rarefactions, cannot be polarised). (c) They provide valuable seconds that can save lives and infrastructure, particularly for automated responses, but are limited close to the epicentre.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] d/3.8 − d/6.0 = 45 (M1); d = 466 km (A1). (b) [4 marks] In transverse waves the medium oscillates perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer (crests and troughs, can be polarised); in longitudinal waves it oscillates parallel to it (compressions and rarefactions, cannot be polarised). (c) [4 marks] For: P-waves travel faster than the damaging S- and surface waves, giving seconds of warning; automatic train stopping and gas shut-off in Japan and Mexico. Against: warning time is short close to the epicentre; false alarms reduce public trust; expensive dense sensor networks are needed. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: They provide valuable seconds that can save lives and infrastructure, particularly for automated responses, but are limited close to the epicentre.

items.stem:
This question is about displacement-distance and displacement-time graphs of waves.

(a) A displacement–time graph for a point on a sound wave shows 4 complete cycles in 20 ms. Calculate the frequency. [2]

(b) With the help of a specific example, explain how the direction of motion of a point on a transverse wave can be found from a displacement–distance graph. [3]

(c) Evaluate the claim: "Graphs are a better way than equations to describe waves." [4]
items.answer: (a) 200 Hz (b) Shift the snapshot a small distance in the direction of travel; the point moves to the displacement of the wave that now occupies its position, so points ahead of a crest move up and points behind it move down. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) Graphs and equations complement each other: graphs aid understanding and data reading, equations allow precise calculation.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] T = 0.02/4 (M1); f = 1/T = 200 Hz (A1). (b) [3 marks] Shift the snapshot a small distance in the direction of travel; the point moves to the displacement of the wave that now occupies its position, so points ahead of a crest move up and points behind it move down. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (c) [4 marks] For: graphs make wavelength, period and phase visible; easy to compare snapshots. Against: equations y = A sin(2π(x/λ − t/T)) contain all information compactly; calculations need equations; graphs can be misread (confusing the two types). Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Graphs and equations complement each other: graphs aid understanding and data reading, equations allow precise calculation.

items.stem:
This question is about sound waves and electromagnetic waves: nature and speed.

(a) During a storm near Nairobi, thunder is heard 3.0 s after the lightning flash. Estimate the distance to the lightning (speed of sound 340 m s⁻¹). [2]

(b) Explain the difference between sound waves and electromagnetic waves. [4]

(c) "Ultrasound imaging is safer than X-ray imaging and should always be preferred." Discuss this view, referring to the physics of sound waves and electromagnetic waves. [6]
items.answer: (a) 1020 m (b) Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves that need a medium and travel at hundreds to thousands of m s⁻¹; EM waves are transverse oscillating fields that travel through a vacuum at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. (c) Ultrasound is preferred where it gives adequate images (pregnancy, soft tissue), but X-rays remain necessary for bone and some diagnoses.
items.markingKey: (a) [2 marks] d = vt (light travel time negligible) (M1) = 1020 m (A1). (b) [4 marks] Sound waves are longitudinal mechanical waves that need a medium and travel at hundreds to thousands of m s⁻¹; EM waves are transverse oscillating fields that travel through a vacuum at 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. (c) [6 marks] For: ultrasound is non-ionising – no known cancer risk; real-time imaging, cheap and portable. Against: ultrasound cannot image through bone or air well (lungs, brain); lower resolution for some applications; X-ray CT gives detailed 3D images of bone. Award the final mark(s) for a judgement supported by the arguments: Ultrasound is preferred where it gives adequate images (pregnancy, soft tissue), but X-rays remain necessary for bone and some diagnoses.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "rarefaction"?

The time for one complete oscillation of a point on the wave, T = 1/f
A "snapshot" graph showing the displacement of every point along a wave at one instant; the wavelength can be read from it

items.answer: A region of a longitudinal wave where the particles are further apart than normal (lower pressure)

items.stem: Explain how seismic waves provide evidence that Earth’s outer core is liquid.
items.answer: Transverse S-waves are not detected in a shadow zone on the far side of Earth; since liquids cannot transmit shear (transverse) waves, the outer core must be liquid.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a displacement–distance graph and a displacement–time graph.
items.answer: A displacement–distance graph is a snapshot of all points at one instant and shows the wavelength; a displacement–time graph follows one point over time and shows the period.
items.markingKey: A displacement–distance graph is a snapshot of all points at one instant and shows the wavelength; a displacement–time graph follows one point over time and shows the period. items.stem: "Ultrasound imaging is safer than X-ray imaging and should always be preferred." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
